opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of the more interesting things we worked on early on. One of the first lessons was that the model often knows more about its own limitations than you'd expect, but it doesn't spontaneously express that knowledge. If you just train it to imitate confident human-written answers, it learns to sound confident regardless of whether it actually knows the answer. So a lot of the hallucination problem was less about the model lacking knowledge and more about the training objective not rewarding honesty about uncertainty.

What we found was that you could get surprisingly far with a relatively small amount of targeted data: examples where the right behavior is to say "I don't have access to the internet," or "I can't actually run code," or "I'm not sure about this." The model generalizes from those examples reasonably well, which suggests there's some internal representation of "this is something I can or can't do" that the fine-tuning is latching onto.

The tricky part is calibration, getting the balance right. If you push too hard, the model becomes overly cautious and starts refusing or hedging on things it actually can do well, which is really annoying for users. If you don't push enough, it confidently makes things up. And the line moves as the model gets more capable, so the behavior you trained on one version doesn't necessarily transfer cleanly to the next. You have to keep revisiting it.

I think the deeper lesson was that a lot of what we call "alignment" in these early systems was really about getting the model to accurately represent itself: what it is, what it can do, what it knows. That's a precondition for it being genuinely helpful. You can't trust an assistant that doesn't know where its own competence ends.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the more interesting problems we ran into early on. The thing you have to understand is that the base model doesn't actually have a notion of itself. It's trained to predict text, and it has a lot of latent knowledge about the world, but it doesn't know what it is or what it can and can't do. So when you turn it into a chatbot, you have to teach it that somehow.

And the naive thing you might do is just write a bunch of examples where the model says "I'm an AI language model, I can't browse the internet, I don't have access to real-time information," and so on. And that works to some extent. But what we found is that the model would generalize in weird ways. It would learn the pattern of saying "I can't do that" and then apply it to things it actually could do. Or you'd have the opposite problem, where it would confidently claim to have done something, like looked up a web page or run some code, when it had no ability to do that at all. It would just hallucinate the result.

So one of the big lessons was that you really have to think about what the model's actual capabilities are, and your training data has to be consistent with that. If you have examples where the model claims to know something it couldn't possibly know, or refuses something it can handle fine, you're teaching it a kind of incoherent self-model, and that leaks everywhere.

The other lesson, which I think is more subtle, is about calibration. There's a lot of knowledge inside the model about what it knows. You can see this if you look at the probabilities it assigns. It's often reasonably well calibrated at the token level. But the chat behavior you get out of supervised fine-tuning tends to destroy that. If your human demonstrators always write confident answers, the model learns to always write confident answers, regardless of whether it actually knows the thing. And that's where a lot of the hallucination problem comes from. It's not that the model is incapable of knowing its limits; it's that the training process can teach it to ignore them.

That's part of why I became more interested in RL for this. With RL, you can actually reward the model for saying "I'm not sure" when it's genuinely uncertain, and penalize it for making stuff up, and the model can learn to use its own internal sense of confidence rather than just imitating a style. Whereas with pure imitation, you're kind of stuck with whatever the demonstrators did, and the demonstrators don't have access to what the model knows.

So I'd say the big takeaway was that teaching a model its limitations isn't really a matter of writing the right disclaimers. It's about making the whole training signal consistent with what the model actually is, and finding ways to let the model's own internal knowledge about its uncertainty come through, instead of overwriting it.

r002.rationale: It says the model generalized the “I can’t do that” pattern to things it actually could do, describing limitations extending beyond the training examples.

astra-6.text:
One thing we learned was that recognizing your limitations isn’t a single capability. The model might be able to say, “I can’t browse the internet,” but that doesn’t mean it reliably knows when it’s answering a question incorrectly. Those are quite different problems.

And there’s a tension in how you train this. If you reward the model for being cautious, it can learn to hedge all the time. That might look like humility, but it isn’t necessarily good calibration. You want it to answer directly when it has a good basis for answering, and express uncertainty when it doesn’t.

So the challenge is getting that uncertainty to track whether the answer is actually reliable, rather than just teaching the model a particular way of talking.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing that surprised me was how hard it is to teach the model when to say, “I don’t know.” With early ChatGPT, we wanted it to acknowledge its limitations, but that isn’t just a matter of teaching it a phrase. It has to distinguish questions it can answer from questions where it’s likely to make something up.

And the feedback can push you in either direction. If you reward answers that look helpful and complete, you can encourage confident guessing. If you reward caution too much, you get a model that refuses questions it could have answered. So the goal is calibration: being useful while expressing uncertainty where it actually matters.

I think the broader lesson was that getting the model to talk about its limitations is much easier than getting its behavior to reliably reflect those limitations.
